Benfieldside Primary School improved its licensed deficit by £57,000 (from £0.241 million to £0.183 million). However, Q1 forecast does not include teachers' pay award impact. Budget assumed 3.25% award with 25% grant coverage; government confirmed 3.5% with 70% grant coverage, requiring schools to fund 30% of increase vs 25% budgeted. Individual school estimates will be updated at Q2 forecast.
findings.matters: Signals emerging school viability concerns; indicates late-confirmed grants masked underlying pressures; teachers' pay award impact will change position at Q2 and some schools will face budget stress
findings.figures: Fewer than ten schools in deficit; Benfieldside Primary improvement £57,000; pay award 3.5% vs 3.25% budgeted; schools to fund 30% of increase vs 25% budgeted
findings.quote: The forecast position at individual school level indicates that a small number of schools (less than ten) may be in deficit at the end of the current financial year and a more significant number of schools may not have sufficient reserves available to set a balanced budget in 2027/28.

findings.committee: Children and Young People's Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Overview and Scrutiny - CYPS Q1 Forecast of Outturn 2026-27
findings.headline: NHS continuing care contributions for complex needs placements forecast at £1.968 million against budget of £2.900 million, a £0.932 million income shortfall
findings.detail: Continuing care packages support children with long-term complex health needs arising from disability, accident or illness that cannot be met by social care alone. The income shortfall reflects lower than expected contributions from health partners despite increasing levels of complex need in the system. Council is reviewing whether additional cases qualify for Integrated Care Board funding and investigating why applications have been refused, expressing concern that "financial pressures within the ICB has resulted in these applications being unfairly refused when compared to previous cases." Regional review of Continuing Health Care, Continuing Care, and related pathways is underway, which could represent risk or opportunity depending on outcome.
findings.matters: Council income dependent on health partner commissioning decisions; demonstrates vulnerability to ICB budget pressures; regional review may affect future-year funding sustainability; fairness concerns over application decisions
findings.figures: Budgeted income £2.900 million; forecast income £1.968 million; shortfall £0.932 million
findings.quote: An annual income budget of £2.900 million was set for 2026/27, based on recent trends and the increasing levels of complex need in the system that attract continuing health care contributions. The forecast income for 2026/27 is £1.968 million, which results in a shortfall of £0.932 million against the budgeted assumption.

findings.committee: Children and Young People's Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Overview and Scrutiny - CYPS Q1 Forecast of Outturn 2026-27
findings.headline: Durham Cares Programme cost-avoidance savings of £6.8 million forecast to underdeliver in 2026-27, with in-house supported accommodation scheme delayed until 2027-28, creating £3.864 million net overspend in Children Looked After placements
findings.detail: Council planned £6.8 million of CLA placement cost-avoidance savings for 2026-27 through Durham Cares Programme. Delays in in-house accommodation (delays to Ofsted registration and recruitment) mean the service will not be fully operational until 2027-28. This creates £3.864 million net overspend: external residential £0.823 million over budget (144 placements forecast vs 144 budgeted but average cost trending upward); crisis intervention/unregistered £2.778 million over budget (18 placements vs 14 budgeted); offset by in-house residential £1.525 million under budget (delays to new homes being available). The report clarifies this is a timing issue rather than demand outstripping budget.
findings.matters: Planned mitigation delivering less than forecast creates in-year cash pressure and extends savings timeline; programme targets £31 million across full MTFP; timing slippage may cascade if not resolved
findings.figures: £6.8 million planned savings; £3.864 million net CLA placement overspend; £31 million MTFP target; external residential overspend £0.823 million; crisis intervention overspend £2.778 million
findings.quote: There is a forecast overspend of £3.864 million against the CLA placements budget this year based on the forecasts prepared at 30 June 2026. Unlike previous years, the overspend is not as a result of demand and unit costs outstripping the base budget assumptions, rather it is a timing issue in terms of the delivery of the demand management and cost avoidance mitigation measures that were factored into the base budget around sufficiency of residential homes and specifically in getting the in-house supported accommodation scheme up and running.

findings.committee: Children and Young People's Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Overview and Scrutiny - CYPS Q1 Forecast of Outturn 2026-27

The EHIVC service overall overspend of £1.723 million is almost entirely attributable to the ASC deficit of £1.905 million, partially offset by £0.186 million reserve drawdown. Additional income provision targeting complex needs (unavailable elsewhere) is planned from September 2026 with £0.750 million forecast income.
findings.matters: An Ofsted inspection outcome directly translated into material service income loss within same financial year; recovery depends on occupancy reaching 82% by November 2026, a forecast that must materialize within-year to avoid increased reserve drawdown

findings.paper_title: Overview and Scrutiny - CYPS Q1 Forecast of Outturn 2026-27
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block deficit increases from budgeted £30.278 million to forecast £31.105 million; cumulative DSG reserve forecast to reach £67.185 million deficit by 31 March 2027, contingent on SEND Local Area Reform Plan approval
findings.detail: The High Needs Block was budgeted with a structural deficit of £30.278 million. Q1 forecast widens this by £0.827 million to £31.105 million due to higher numbers of special school places and elevated costs for pupils with complex needs. The cumulative DSG reserve moves from opening deficit of £36.080 million to £67.185 million deficit forecast. Subject to SEND Local Area Reform Plan approval, 90% of the initial deficit (£32.472 million) could be released, reducing cumulative position to £34.785 million. The statutory override allowing this treatment expires 31 March 2028, when central government assumes SEND funding responsibility.
findings.matters: The largest structural financial pressure facing the council; defines the balance sheet position at end of MTFP; contingent on external approval processes beyond council control and dependent on central government policy change
findings.figures: Budgeted HNB deficit £30.278 million, forecast £31.105 million; cumulative reserve £36.080 million opening to £67.185 million forecast (£34.785 million if LARP approved); override expires March 2028

findings.committee: Children and Young People's Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Overview and Scrutiny - CYPS Final Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Maintained schools reversed quarter three deficit forecast, contributing net £2.721 million to reserves in 2025-26, but five schools ended year in deficit with one (Benfieldside Primary) requiring licensed deficit budget
findings.detail: The 123 maintained schools as a group made a net contribution to reserves of £2.721 million in 2025-26, a material improvement from the quarter three forecast which anticipated the schools would use £5.491 million of reserves. Total school reserves at 31 March 2026 stood at £29.476 million (compared to opening balance of £26.755 million). Of 123 schools, 81 contributed a combined £5.962 million to reserves while 42 used £3.241 million, producing the net contribution. However, five schools individually ended the year in deficit. Four 'have set a budget in 2026/27 which will result in each school ending the 2026/27 financial year in a surplus position, whilst one school (Benfieldside Primary) are unable to do this and have required a licensed deficit budget to be agreed to allow them the time bring their budget back into balance over a longer period.'
findings.matters: School reserves are a key health indicator for the school system. The improvement in aggregate position and the reversal of Q3 deficit forecast is positive, but the existence of five deficit schools and one requiring a licensed deficit arrangement indicates targeted intervention is needed at individual schools. For a finance director, this signals whether school-level budget management is sound or whether central support is being pulled into struggling schools.
findings.figures: Net contribution to reserves £2.721m (vs Q3 forecast use of £5.491m); total reserves £29.476m; 5 schools in deficit; 4 with recovery plans for 2026/27; 1 (Benfieldside Primary) with licensed deficit
findings.quote: Of the 123 maintained schools remaining at 31 March 2026, 81 schools contributed a combined £5.962 million to reserves in year and 42 schools used a combined £3.241 million of reserves during the year, resulting in the net contribution of £2.721 million...Five schools ended the year in an overall deficit position. Four of these schools have set a budget in 2026/27 which will result in each school ending the 2026/27 financial year in a surplus position, whilst one school (Benfieldside Primary) are unable to do this and have required a licensed deficit budget to be agreed

findings.committee: Children and Young People's Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Overview and Scrutiny - CYPS Final Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Home to School Transport delivered £4.625 million underspend (12% of £38.771 million budget) through tendering exercises and service transformation, though £2.1 million is already factored into 2026/27 base budget
findings.detail: HTST underspent by £4.625 million with underspends across all transport types. The report attributes this to: successful tendering exercises over summer 2025 'where the impact of significant work with providers and route optimisation helped to minimise cost increases'; fuel price stability; reduced single-person journeys with increased group travel (£0.380m saving); and increased personal travel budgets allowing parents to provide transport (£0.332m saving). However, the council has already embedded much of this gain into next year's plans: 'An element of the underspend (circa £2.1 million) against the Home to School Transport budget was factored into the 2026/27 base budget, where the previously anticipated cost pressures were reduced from an originally forecast budget uplift of £1.490 million to a budget reduction of £0.600 million in 2026/27.'
findings.matters: This demonstrates effective demand management and supplier negotiation in a cost-intensive service. Other councils facing transport cost pressures would want evidence of whether similar tendering and route optimisation can be replicated. However, the second part of the story matters equally: the council has already committed most of the saving to future-year budget reductions, limiting its ability to use this performance to offset other pressures. For lenders, it shows competent operational management but also tight budget discipline.
findings.figures: HTST underspend £4.625m on £38.771m budget (12%); group travel saving £0.380m; personal travel budget saving £0.332m; £2.1m of underspend embedded in 2026/27; budget change from +£1.490m uplift to -£0.600m reduction
findings.quote: An element of the underspend (circa £2.1 million) against the Home to School Transport budget was factored into the 2026/27 base budget, where the previously anticipated cost pressures were reduced from an originally forecast budget uplift of £1.490 million to a budget reduction of £0.600 million in 2026/27.

findings.committee: Children and Young People's Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Overview and Scrutiny - CYPS Final Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Children's Social Care reported £8.582 million overspends outside CLA placements, including £3.7 million staffing overspend linked to improved retention rates and agency staffing for caseload demand
findings.detail: Beyond CLA placement costs, Children's Social Care faced multiple pressures. Staffing overspend reached £3.7 million for Children in Care and Supporting Permanence teams, up from £3.3 million Q3 forecast, 'where improved retention rates, alongside the need to recruit to additional agency staffing to manage caseload demand pressures have resulted in staffing spending exceeding budget.' Other pressures included: care leavers £0.913m overspend (reduced UASC grant when young people turn 18); family support £0.547m overspend (children at risk of entering care); transport £0.740m overspend (difficulty recruiting drivers, increased taxi reliance); disabled children adaptations £0.967m; Staying Put £0.376m; Children in Need support £0.469m; legal costs £0.299m; and care leaver university support £0.200m. The staffing pressure is flagged as structural: 'The overall staffing position is currently being reviewed in conjunction with plans to deliver Social Care reforms that are due to take effect from April 2027, which is likely to necessitate some budget growth in 2027/28 as part of MTFP(17).'
findings.matters: A finance director must understand whether these are one-off costs or structural pressures requiring permanent budget growth. The explicit flag that staffing growth is 'likely' to be needed in MTFP(17) signals the council's assessment that this cannot be absorbed from efficiency gains. Other councils facing similar child social care staffing pressures need this evidence. For lenders, it indicates whether children's services budgets are at sustainable levels.
findings.figures: Staffing overspend £3.7m (up from £3.3m Q3 forecast); care leavers £0.913m; family support £0.547m; transport £0.740m; adaptations £0.967m; total other pressures £8.582m
findings.quote: £3.7 million overspend in Social Worker staffing, relating to Children in Care and Supporting Permanence teams, where improved retention rates, alongside the need to recruit to additional agency staffing to manage caseload demand pressures have resulted in staffing spending exceeding budget...The overall staffing position is currently being reviewed in conjunction with plans to deliver Social Care reforms that are due to take effect from April 2027, which is likely to necessitate some budget growth in 2027/28 as part of MTFP(17)

findings.committee: Children and Young People's Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Overview and Scrutiny - CYPS Final Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Aycliffe Secure Centre depleted £0.710 million of reserves following December 2025 'Inadequate' Ofsted rating, with remaining reserves of £0.186 million insufficient for forecast continued deficit in 2026/27
findings.detail: Following an 'Inadequate' Ofsted inspection in December 2025 (rating later improved to 'Requires Improvement' in March 2026), bed occupancy dropped during the final quarter, resulting in income significantly lower than budget. The service used £0.710 million of earmarked reserves to balance its 2025-26 position. Remaining reserves stand at £0.186 million. The report states: 'it is likely the in-year deficit will exceed this level, resulting in a financial pressure for the wider CYPS budget next year, which may require corporate support through centrally held contingencies and / or through the General Fund Reserve.'
findings.matters: A finance director and lenders need to assess whether an Ofsted recovery plan can restore occupancy, or whether the facility will require ongoing subsidy. The explicit flag that reserves are insufficient and corporate bailout may be needed signals a budget pressure in 2026-27. For other councils, this shows the financial consequence of a significant inspection downgrade.
findings.figures: Reserve depletion £0.710m; remaining reserves £0.186m; described as 'likely' to exceed this in 2026/27
findings.quote: Following the 'Inadequate' Ofsted judgement from the inspection in December 2025, with Ofsted reassessing the position in March 2026 and improving the rating to 'Requires Improvement' on the strength of the progress made against the actions to address the concerns raised in December 2025...it is likely the in-year deficit will exceed this level, resulting in a financial pressure for the wider CYPS budget next year, which may require corporate support through centrally held contingencies and / or through the General Fund Reserve.

findings.committee: Children and Young People's Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Overview and Scrutiny - CYPS Final Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: High Needs DSG block deficit widened to £39.723 million from £22.981 million at start of year; recovery of 90% is conditional on DfE approval of Local SEND Reform Plan submitted June 2026
findings.detail: The High Needs Block overspent by £16.742 million in 2025-26, worse than the budgeted deficit of £14.250 million by £2.492 million and worse than Q3 forecast. Drivers included Post-16 Independent and Non-Maintained Special Schools overspend of £0.830 million due to demand higher than anticipated, and Alternative Provision overspend of £1.754 million (including The Woodlands £0.841m and children Educated Other Than In School £0.984m, described as 'an enduring pressure into 2026/27'). The centrally retained DSG reserve deficit deteriorated from -£20.229 million to -£36.080 million. The council's funding recovery depends on: 'Once the plan is assessed and approved, funding equivalent to a maximum of 90% of the Total DSG Unusable reserve (i.e. £36.080 million) will be payable to the council, which will reduce the overall deficit position to circa £3.6 million.'
findings.matters: The DSG deficit is a material balance sheet liability. If the DfE plan is not approved or approved for less than 90%, the council must absorb the remaining deficit. Other councils facing similar SEND cost pressures need evidence of whether funding recovery is probable. For lenders, this is a significant contingent liability and test of the council's relationship with DfE.
findings.figures: High Needs overspend £16.742m vs budgeted £14.250m deficit; worse than Q3 forecast by £2.492m; Alternative Provision overspend £1.754m; total DSG deficit £36.080m; potential DfE recovery up to 90% of £36.080m
findings.quote: Once the plan is assessed and approved, funding equivalent to a maximum of 90% of the Total DSG Unusable reserve (i.e. £36.080 million) will be payable to the council, which will reduce the overall deficit position to circa £3.6 million

findings.detail: The largest area of CYPS spending, CLA placements had net budget of £97.346 million (£20.295 million higher than 2024-25, including £4 million transfer from Adult Health Services). The service overspent by £5.588 million. Multiple placement types exceeded budget: External Residential £2.621 million overspend (128 average placements at £0.371m per annum vs budget of 121 at £0.379m), Crisis Intervention £2.045 million overspend (17 average placements at £0.660m vs budgeted 14 at £0.707m), Supported Accommodation £1.598 million, and Independent Fostering Agencies £2.056 million. findings.matters: A finance director needs to understand whether CLA growth and associated cost pressures are structural or temporary, and whether mitigation plans are on track or pose budget risk in 2026/27. Other councils face similar demographic and demand pressures in child safeguarding. For lenders, this signals whether the council's children's services budget baseline is sustainable.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 Budget Strategy Report - Durham - Sept 26
findings.headline: Annual surplus distribution to constituent authorities maintained at £1,041,250 from 2027/28 despite declining cremation volumes
findings.detail: The Joint Committee is maintaining its annual surplus distribution to constituent authorities (Durham County Council £833,000; Spennymoor Town Council £208,250) at current levels from 2027/28 onwards. The distribution has grown from £856,250 in 2022/23 to £1,041,250 by 2026/27. This represents sustained significant dividend extraction during a period of declining demand and upcoming major capital commitments.
findings.matters: Maintaining high dividend payments during demand decline and ahead of major capex limits reserve accumulation and financial flexibility for future uncertainties.
findings.figures: Annual distribution from 2027/28: £1,041,250 (Durham CC £833,000; Spennymoor £208,250); growth from £856,250 (2022/23) to £1,041,250 (2026/27)
findings.quote: The current surplus distributed is £1,041,250 per year (£833,000 to Durham County Council and £208,250 to Spennymoor Town Council). From 2027/28 onwards it is proposed that this will remain the same.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 Budget Strategy Report - Durham - Sept 26
findings.headline: Proposed cremation fee increase to £1,060 in 2027/28 will remain below regional average of £1,062
findings.detail: A fee increase of £35 (3.52%) is proposed for 2027/28, bringing the cremation fee from £1,025 to £1,060. This remains below the current regional average of £1,062 and significantly below the nearest facility at Coundon (£1,265). The fee increase is modest, aligned with inflation assumptions in the council's medium-term financial plan.
findings.matters: Limited pricing power relative to competitors constrains revenue growth options, particularly significant given current demand pressures and declining volumes.

findings.detail: A new planning application has been lodged to change the design of a previously approved crematorium at Castle Eden. Management is monitoring this application to assess competitive impact on both Central Durham and Mountsett Crematoria. This represents an identified risk to future demand at a time when the service is already experiencing volume decline.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 Budget Strategy Report - Durham - Sept 26
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves projected at £3.2 million by March 2029 but will fall to £1.5 million by March 2030 due to Resomation spend
findings.detail: Reserve balances are reported as healthy and sufficient. The forecast shows reserves growing from £2.73 million (March 2027) to a peak of £3.21 million (March 2029), before declining to £1.48 million (March 2030) due to the Resomation capital draw. This significant drawdown reflects the extent to which planned reserves will be deployed for major capital investment.
findings.matters: The reserve trajectory shows how the service is building financial resilience ahead of major capex, but also reveals substantial capital deployment planned within the forecast period.
findings.quote: An updated robust medium-term budget forecast has been produced for the Joint Committee and this demonstrates that the reserve balances of the Joint Committee are still projected to be healthy and sufficient to meet the liabilities and commitments of the Joint Committee for the coming years.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 Budget Strategy Report - Durham - Sept 26
findings.headline: £3 million Resomation project re-profiled to 2029/30 with £1 million funded by DCC loan
findings.detail: The Joint Committee is planning a major capital investment of £3 million for a Resomation system and building extension, originally scheduled for 2027/28–2028/29 but now re-profiled to 2029/30 due to delays in enabling legislation. The project will be funded by £2,087,600 from earmarked reserves and £1 million from a loan from Durham County Council. Law Society review of funerary methods due completion in 2026 may lead to further delay.
findings.matters: The £1 million borrowing represents new debt committed to fund a strategic investment, with timing uncertainty from legislative dependencies.

The service is budgeting conservatively at 2,150 cremations per annum for medium-term planning. This declining trajectory directly affects the revenue base for the service.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet 16.09.26 - QTR1 Forecast of Outturn 2026-27 (003)
findings.headline: Long-term borrowing costs now at 6%+, exceeding council budget assumptions of 5-5.5%, creating headwind as capital programme normalises
findings.detail: Council managing cash position via under-borrowed strategy, with interest payable forecast £4.987m below budget due to capital programme slippage delaying the need to borrow. However, PWLB long-term borrowing rates have risen to above 6%, compared to budget assumptions of 5-5.5%. As capital programme accelerates and cash balances deplete, council will be forced to borrow at higher rates, increasing financing costs. Investment income has overachieved by £2.854m due to higher cash balances and interest rates held at 3.75%, but this is a temporary position subject to MPC decisions.
findings.matters: Rising cost of debt ahead. Under-borrowed position is a timing strategy, not a solution to rate pressures. PWLB rates at 6%+ will materially increase future financing costs as capital spends progress. Limited ability to absorb further capital pressures without borrowing at unfavourable rates.
findings.figures: Long-term borrowing 6%+, budget assumption 5-5.5%, interest payable £4.987m underspend, investment income £2.854m overachievement, net debt £353.914m at 30 June 2026
findings.quote: Long-term borrowing costs are currently standing at above over 6%, which exceeds the Council's assumptions on interest rates on new borrowing of between 5% and 5.5%.

findings.headline: Education and Skills services dependent on NEMSA Single Settlement allocation decision; £0.710m overspend and service running to December 2026 pending outcome
findings.detail: UK Shared Prosperity Funding three-year programme ended March 2025; transition year arrangement concluded. From 2026/27, council dependent on NEMSA (North East Mayoral Strategic Authority) Single Settlement funding for employment and skills services. findings.matters: Service continuity and 2027/28 budget viability contingent on external strategic authority decision outside council control. Significant grant funding transition with planning uncertainty.

findings.headline: Schools facing deficits and insufficient reserves to set balanced budgets in 2027/28, with licensed deficit at Benfieldside Primary
findings.detail: Benfieldside Primary operating under licensed revenue deficit, improved to £0.183m from £0.241m. Council assessment is that small number (fewer than 10) may be in deficit by end of 2026/27, but significantly more schools lack sufficient reserves to set balanced budgets for 2027/28. Teachers' pay award at 3.5% (vs 3.25% budgeted) with schools funding only 30% of the uplift, creating additional unfunded pressure.
findings.matters: Schools deficits cascade to council (Section 251 duty to prevent deficit budgets). Reserve depletion leaves no buffer for inflation or demand shocks in 2027/28. Unfunded pay award creates structural imbalance.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet 16.09.26 - QTR1 Forecast of Outturn 2026-27 (003)
findings.headline: Children's social care placement costs overrunning by £10.278m as demand for external and crisis placements exceeds budget despite sufficiency strategy
findings.detail: CYPS forecast overspend of £10.278m (4.6% of budget) driven primarily by external residential placements (£0.823m over budget) and crisis/unregistered placements (£2.778m over budget). findings.paper_title: Cabinet 16.09.26 - QTR1 Forecast of Outturn 2026-27 (003)
findings.headline: DSG High Needs Block overspend has nearly doubled to £31.105m in year, driving cumulative deficit toward £70.828m
findings.detail: The in-year High Needs overspend of £31.105m is a substantial increase from £16.742m in 2025/26, reflecting additional demand and cash-flat funding. findings.figures: £31.105m in-year overspend, £70.828m cumulative forecast, £39.723m opening deficit, £32.472m stability grant (subject to LARP approval), £11m earmarked reserve, £1.230m interest cost

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report 16.09.26 - MTFP17
findings.headline: Pay award inflation assumptions increased 1% above prior year; pay costs now £3.3m higher than forecast just 6 months ago
findings.detail: The council has raised pay award assumptions from 2.5% to 3.5% for 2027/28 (and increased 2028/29 from 2.0% to 3.0%), citing inflation concerns following Middle East conflict. This creates an additional £3.325 million pressure in 2027/28 alone. Combined with 4.7% National Living Wage growth, this escalates employer cost inflation significantly.
findings.matters: Recent revision of pay assumptions mid-forecast period indicates underlying cost inflation pressures may be worse than expected; suggests forecast confidence is low
findings.figures: Pay award costs: 3.5% for 2027/28 (£10.825m), 3.0% for 2028/29 (£9.150m); £3.325m increase vs MTFP16 in 2027/28; NLW growth assumed at 4.7%
findings.quote: The updated forecasts for pay awards, which are negotiated nationally, are based on an assumed 3.5% pay award in 2027/28 (£10.825 million)... These assumed increases are higher than the assumptions made in MTFP (16), reflecting concerns around rising inflation following the conflict in the Middle East.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report 16.09.26 - MTFP17
findings.headline: Government funding settlement extends only to 2028/29; Recovery Grants potentially withdrawn from 2029/30
findings.detail: The multi-year settlement runs only through 2028/29. Recovery Grant and Recovery Uplift Grant (introduced for 2025/26-2026/27) may not continue beyond 2028/29. If withdrawn, the council could lose funding from the next CSR. Additionally, the new Prime Minister creates uncertainty around whether the 2025 CSR commitments will be honoured; the Chancellor's Budget on 28 October 2026 may alter assumptions.
findings.matters: Government funding assumptions become highly uncertain from 2029/30 onwards; near-term reliance on potentially temporary grant streams reduces revenue certainty
findings.figures: Multi-year settlement covers 2026/27-2028/29 only; Recovery Grants potentially withdrawn from 2029/30; Chancellor's Budget 28 October 2026
findings.quote: An emerging risk will be whether the Government continues to retain its allocation of Recovery Grant and Recovery Uplift Grant – which were introduced by the Government as part of the funding package for local authorities in 2025/26 and 2026/27... if the Government was to withdraw this funding at the end of the current multi-year settlement (from the start of 2029/30), the council could, in net terms, lose funding from a future multi-year settlement from 2029/30.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report 16.09.26 - MTFP17
findings.headline: Budget balance dependent on maximum 4.99% council tax rises; lower rises create cascading deficits of £23-36m
findings.detail: The council's budget relies on annual council tax rises of 4.99% (the maximum without a referendum). At 2% rises, a £36.199 million deficit emerges; at 3%, still £23.177 million. This creates dependency on a politically-constrained decision outside the council's direct control and exposes budget to political risk.
findings.matters: Budget sustainability is contingent on maximum allowable tax rises; any political constraint reduces flexibility and increases reliance on either reserves or further service cuts
findings.figures: At 2% tax rise: £36.199m deficit; at 3% tax rise: £23.177m deficit; maximum allowable: 4.99%
findings.quote: With the maximum allowable annual increase of 4.99% (as assumed by Central Government in the CSR 2025)... a 2% annual increase would result in a budget deficit of £36.199 million to be addressed over the MTFP (17) period, while a 3% annual increase would still leave a budget deficit of £23.177 million.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report 16.09.26 - MTFP17
findings.headline: Only £9.2m of £21.5m savings proposals are sufficiently developed; remainder are aspirational transformation savings subject to consultation
findings.detail: Of the £21.519 million savings proposals, only £9.171 million are ready to implement (mainly 2027/28). The remaining £12.348 million are transformation-led savings still undergoing scoping and consultation, with implementation predominantly from 2028/29. The council has already delivered £301 million in cumulative savings since 2010 and warns that further major savings will force staff cuts affecting frontline services.
findings.matters: Savings plan is contingent on delivery of uncertain transformation benefits; delivery risk is material given history of £301m cuts already made and warnings about frontline impact
findings.figures: £9.171 million sufficiently developed savings; £12.348 million transformation savings pending development; £301 million cumulative savings delivered since 2010
findings.quote: Of this, £9.171 million comprises savings proposals that are sufficiently developed to be implemented at this stage (predominantly in 2027/28), with a further £12.348 million identified as transformation-based savings which remain subject to further development, scoping and detailed consultation.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report 16.09.26 - MTFP17
findings.headline: Fair Pay Agreements introduce £5.5m unfunded liability risk from 2028/29 with cost uncertainty not yet resolved
findings.detail: The council has allocated £5.530 million for adult social care Fair Pay Agreements commencing 2028/29, but explicitly warns that actual costs remain unclear and could exceed the allocation. If the hypothecated grant funding proves insufficient, additional unfunded pressures will emerge after implementation.
findings.matters: Hidden liability on adult social care supplier costs that could materialize mid-MTFP period; budget provision assumes government funding matches costs, but this assumption is unproven
findings.figures: £5.530 million allocated for Fair Pay Agreements from 2028/29
findings.quote: At this stage it remains unclear what the full financial cost will be and whether the hypothecated grant allocation expected to be received in 2028/29 will be sufficient to offset these costs, which is what is assumed in the MTFP (17) forecasts. The risk remains that the current budget growth provision for 2028/29 will not fully cover the full longer-term cost of any eventual fair pay settlement, meaning additional unfunded pressures could emerge.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report 16.09.26 - MTFP17
findings.headline: Adult social care fee pressures of £34.4m over four years exceed dedicated precept revenue of £25.9m, leaving structural funding gap
findings.detail: Budgeted adult social care fee uplifts (driven by National Living Wage rises and CPI) total £34.417 million over the forecast period. The dedicated 2% ASC precept would generate only £25.944 million over the same period, leaving a £8.5m gap. Every 1% increase in National Living Wage alone adds £1.5 million to ASC costs, and the council assumes 4.7% NLW growth in 2027/28.
findings.matters: Unfunded structural gap in adult social care indicates demand cost growth outpacing both general funding and dedicated precept revenue; trend will worsen as population ages
findings.figures: £34.417 million ASC fee uplift costs; £25.944 million ASC precept revenue; 4.7% NLW growth assumed for 2027/28; every 1% NLW increase = £1.5m cost
findings.quote: The budget growth required to fund adult social care fee uplifts is £11.156 million in 2027/28, £9.467 million in 2028/29, £8.086 million in 2029/30 and £5.708 million in 2030/31 – a total estimated cost pressure of £34.417 million across the next four years.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report 16.09.26 - MTFP17
findings.headline: Two-year cash deficit of £49.7m exceeds available reserves of £34.6m, creating risk of forced recourse to Exceptional Financial Support
findings.detail: The cumulative cash deficit in 2027/28 and 2028/29 alone (£49.703 million) exceeds the council's unallocated MTFP Support Reserve (£34.576 million). The council explicitly warns that authorities over-reliant on reserves have been forced into Exceptional Financial Support regimes, where central government removes local control. EFS took 29 councils in 2025/26, rising to 36 in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion below two-year deficit creates near-term solvency risk and escalates likelihood of loss of financial autonomy
findings.figures: £49.703 million cumulative cash deficit 2027/28-2028/29; £34.576 million unallocated MTFP reserve; 36 councils in EFS in 2026/27 (up from 29 in 2025/26)
findings.quote: This cash deficit exceeds the unallocated MTFP Support Reserve of £34.576 million. It is not financially sustainable to place an over-reliance on reserves to balance the budget, therefore further sustainable measures from either council tax or further savings will be required to secure a balanced financial position.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Report 16.09.26 - MTFP17
findings.headline: Budget deficit has grown by £38.9m since last year's forecast, with £83.7m shortfall over four years before new savings
findings.detail: The council now forecasts a £83.662 million deficit over 2027/28-2030/31, compared to the position assumed in MTFP16. This is £38.917 million worse than previously expected. Even after applying £21.519 million of new savings proposals, a £62.143 million residual deficit remains, requiring either significant council tax rises or deeper cuts.
findings.matters: Growing structural deficits indicate worsening financial sustainability and increasing reliance on discretionary actions (tax rises or reserves) to avoid distress
findings.figures: £83.662 million deficit over four years; £38.917 million deterioration since MTFP16; residual deficit of £62.143 million after savings
findings.quote: Before any new MTFP (17) savings or council tax increases are applied, the forecast budget deficit / savings requirement is £83.662 million over the four-year period 2027/28 to 2030/31. This position is £38.917 million higher than the previous MTFP(16) planning assumptions.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 - Changing Together Strategic Business Case
findings.headline: The council has identified insufficient delivery capacity as a material risk to the transformation programme.
findings.detail: The paper identifies that the programme could slow or rely too heavily on already stretched services if delivery capacity is insufficient. The mitigation proposed is a capacity plan and prioritization, but the council is acknowledging that it may not have the organizational capacity to execute the scale of change required.
findings.matters: Transformation programmes are often delayed or scaled back due to lack of available capacity to deliver change alongside business as usual. If the council's services are already under strain, adding a major transformation programme on top creates implementation risk and could impact service quality during the transition.
findings.figures: No specific capacity metrics provided
findings.quote: Insufficient delivery capacity. Programme slows or relies too heavily on already stretched services.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 - Changing Together Strategic Business Case
findings.headline: Oracle Fusion and digital transformation are central to the savings and redesign plan, creating delivery dependency risk.
findings.detail: The paper identifies Oracle Fusion as a major enabler of back-office transformation and lists as a key risk that Oracle Fusion, digital, data or AI dependencies are underestimated, with potential for benefits to be delayed or service redesign to be constrained. Digital capability is positioned as essential to closing the MTFP gap.
findings.matters: If a significant portion of the council's financial sustainability plan depends on a major IT transformation delivering on time and on budget, and that programme itself has delivery risk, the council's ability to realize savings is constrained by external programme dependencies. Implementation risk on Oracle Fusion translates directly to MTFP realization risk.
findings.figures: No cost figures for Oracle Fusion provided in this document
findings.quote: Oracle Fusion, digital, data or AI dependencies are underestimated. Benefits are delayed or service redesign is constrained.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 - Changing Together Strategic Business Case
findings.headline: The council has identified a material risk that savings will be overestimated or not deliverable, leaving the MTFP gap unresolved.
findings.detail: In its risk assessment, the council explicitly flags that savings could be overestimated or undeliverable, with potential impact that the MTFP gap remains unresolved and confidence in the programme reduces. This is the council's own acknowledgment of realization risk in its transformation plans.
findings.matters: A council that is candid about delivery risk on its own plans is more credible, but this is also a red flag for lenders: if the council cannot deliver these savings, what is the fallback position? This is the core dependency between the transformation programme and financial sustainability.
findings.figures: No specific figures; risk is qualitative
findings.quote: Savings are overestimated or not deliverable. MTFP gap remains unresolved and confidence in the programme reduces.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 - Changing Together Strategic Business Case
findings.headline: Growing demand pressures in children's and adults' social care, where prevention and early intervention are critical.
findings.detail: The paper identifies that services are experiencing increasing complexity, volume and cost of demand, with particular pressure in areas such as children's and adults' social care. The council recognizes these are demand-driven cost pressures requiring prevention and early intervention strategies.
findings.matters: Social care is the largest single area of council spending and these are largely non-discretionary costs. Demand-driven cost growth that outpaces population or demographics is a material financial risk, and the council's ability to manage it through prevention determines medium-term affordability.
findings.figures: No specific spend figures provided for social care demand growth
findings.quote: Services are experiencing increasing complexity, volume and cost of demand, particularly in areas such as children's and adults' social care where prevention and early intervention are critical.

findings.headline: A £88m four-year MTFP deficit with only £21m of solutions identified so far.
findings.detail: The council faces a forecasted budget deficit of approximately £88m before any new MTFP savings or council tax assumptions. Service reviews have identified more than £21m of savings to date, leaving a significant gap that must be closed through the wider transformation programme. The council acknowledges this requires more than incremental changes.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the scale of financial pressure the council faces and whether the council's response plan has credible pathways to close the gap. With less than 25% of the deficit addressed, the realization risk is material.
findings.figures: Forecasted budget deficit of c. £88m; more than £21m of savings identified through service review activity
findings.quote: The Council is managing a significant four-year MTFP challenge, with a forecasted budget deficit of c. £88m, before any new MTFP (17) savings or council tax assumptions are applied. More than £21m of savings have been identified through service review activity.

The council is responding through in-house fostering and specialist homes, but this is identified as a pressure area requiring active management.

findings.committee: Economy and Enterprise Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: E&E OSC Q4 Rev Cap Outturn 25-26
findings.headline: Council ended service cash limit arrangements and centralised reserve oversight from April 2025
findings.detail: From 1 April 2025, the council ended its service-level cash limit reserve and accounting arrangements following changes to Financial Procedure Rules approved by Full Council in March 2025. All budget variances and financial activity are now accounted for within individual service grouping areas and directly aligned to services rather than tracked via separate cash limit arrangements. This represents a shift toward centralised corporate-level oversight of reserve movements.
findings.matters: Structural changes to financial governance and reserve management affect how a council controls and reports its financial position. For lenders, stronger corporate-level oversight of reserves can indicate improved governance, though implementation of new financial reporting structures carries transition risks.

findings.committee: Economy and Enterprise Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: E&E OSC Q4 Rev Cap Outturn 25-26
findings.headline: Single Homelessness Accommodation Programme generating revenue overspend due to delays in bringing properties into use
findings.detail: The SHAP project generated a revenue overspend of £0.208m because delays in bringing new properties into use deferred the generation of rental income expected to offset programme costs. Capital expenditure on the programme was reprofiled by £0.670m with completion extended to 30 June 2026. This programme therefore shows both revenue cost pressure and capital delivery delays, with income generation being deferred.
findings.matters: A programme showing both revenue cost overspend and capital delays, coupled with deferred income, signals material delivery risks. For lenders, the combination of overspending and delayed income generation raises questions about the council's ability to generate expected revenues to offset programme costs.

For lenders, this raises questions about the council's ability to deliver planned schemes within forecast timescales.
