findings.headline: County Durham's cash reserves have been depleted by SEND funding shortfalls and depend on conditional government grants to be replenished.
findings.detail: The council states that its "cash reserves... have been depleted as a result of having to bank-roll the shortfall in funding sustained over recent years". Reserves are expected to be replenished only upon receipt of the High Needs Stability Grant, which is conditional on the council submitting and securing DfE approval of a Local SEND Reform Plan. This creates dependence on conditional funding to restore liquidity.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves reduce financial flexibility and liquidity to manage unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls; dependence on conditional government funding to replenish reserves creates execution risk.
findings.figures: Specific reserve balance not stated; lost interest on deployed reserves cumulative over multiple years and on future deficits through 2028.
findings.quote: The eventual receipt of the HNSG will replenish the Council's cash reserves, which have been depleted as a result of having to bank-roll the shortfall in funding sustained over recent years, which is costing the council taxpayers in County Durham in terms of lost interest.

findings.paper_title: 06 Draft Annual Governance Statement 202526
findings.headline: County Durham is formalising new governance actions for Children's Services (Aycliffe Secure Centre, mental health) and SEND for 2026-27, indicating prior control weaknesses in high-cost services.
findings.detail: The council has identified four new governance improvement actions for 2026-27, in addition to four carried forward from prior years. New actions target governance strengthening in Aycliffe Secure Centre, children's mental health, SEND reform, and planning governance. The formal identification of governance actions in these areas, particularly in Children's Services, is a signal that prior control or assurance gaps exist.
findings.matters: Children's Services and SEND are material cost areas; new governance actions indicate prior control weaknesses that may affect service delivery, financial control, or regulatory standing.
findings.figures: 8 governance improvement actions for 2026-27 (4 carried forward, 4 new); Aycliffe Secure Centre, children's mental health, and SEND are three of the new governance action areas.
findings.quote: Action 5 (New Governance Action for 2026-27) - Children & Young People's Services: Strengthen governance oversight, assurance and risk management arrangements in relation to Aycliffe Secure Centre.

findings.paper_title: 06 Draft Annual Governance Statement 202526
findings.headline: County Durham's internal auditor gave a Moderate overall assurance opinion for 2025-26, indicating control weaknesses exist, and audit coverage was reduced by workforce constraints.
findings.detail: The Chief Internal Auditor concluded the council achieved a Moderate overall assurance opinion based on "substantial or moderate assurance ratings across all audits completed during the year". This is not an unqualified opinion. Concurrently, the council identifies "Workforce capacity and recruitment challenges, contributing to reduced internal audit coverage" as a governance pressure. A Moderate opinion with reduced assurance coverage means some control testing was not completed and some control weaknesses may not have been identified.
findings.matters: Internal audit is the primary internal assurance function; a Moderate opinion signals control gaps exist; reduced coverage from staffing constraints means audit risk is elevated.
findings.figures: Moderate overall assurance opinion; core control system rated sound but areas identified requiring strengthening; internal audit coverage reduced due to workforce constraints.
findings.quote: Internal Audit provided a Moderate overall assurance opinion, confirming that the core system of internal control is sound with some areas requiring strengthening.

findings.paper_title: 06 Draft Annual Governance Statement 202526
findings.headline: County Durham faces a £44.745m funding gap across 2027-28 to 2029-30 but has identified only £0.954m of new savings for those years, requiring future council tax rises or service cuts.
findings.detail: The council balanced 2026-27 through £9.1m of new savings and a 1.99% council tax rise. However, it has identified only £10.057m of new savings across the four-year period, with £9.103m (90%) planned for 2026-27. This leaves £0.954m for 2027-30 combined, against a projected gap of £44.745m. The council notes it is "currently updating its financial assumptions" for the next MTFP, suggesting the gap may grow. The shortfall between identified savings and the gap implies councils will rely on further tax increases, service reductions, or reserves to balance future budgets.
findings.matters: The savings plan does not cover the structural gap; future budget sustainability depends on further tax rises or service reductions, both of which create financial or operational risk.
findings.figures: £10.057m new savings identified 2026-30; £9.103m planned for 2026-27; £0.954m remaining for 2027-30; £44.745m gap 2027-28 to 2029-30; 1.99% council tax increase 2026-27.
findings.quote: The Council still faces a projected funding gap across the later three years of the MTFP (16) period of £44.745 million - between the years 2027/28 and 2029/30.

findings.paper_title: 06 Draft Annual Governance Statement 202526
findings.headline: County Durham has accumulated a £40m SEND deficit by March 2026, masked by a Statutory Override that expires 31 March 2028, with government relief conditional and post-2028 liability undefined.
findings.detail: The High Needs Block has run annual overspends every year since 2016-17 due to rising demand for children with special educational needs and insufficient central government funding. The 2025-26 in-year deficit is £17m. The cumulative deficit of £40m is hidden from the General Fund by a Statutory Override (expiring March 2028). Government will fund 90% of accumulated deficits to end-2027-28 through the High Needs Stability Grant, but only if the council's Local SEND Reform Plan is approved annually. From April 2028 the government takes on SEND funding directly, but "it remains unclear if local authorities will continue to bear some financial risks around a mismatch between local demand and DfE funding from 2028/29 onwards", creating material budget uncertainty beyond the override expiry.
findings.matters: A £40m liability, even partially relieved by government, is material to credit assessment; relief is conditional and temporary; residual post-2028 risk is undefined.
findings.figures: £17m in-year deficit 2025-26; £40m cumulative deficit forecast 31 March 2026; £107.996m HNB funding 2026-27 (no increase from prior year); government to fund 90% of deficits to end-2027-28; Statutory Override ends 31 March 2028.
findings.quote: In each year since 2016/17 (barring 2022/23 when there was a small underspend), there has been a recurring in-year overspend of HNB expenditure against HNB grant allocations in Durham.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Treasury Management Final Outturn
findings.headline: Average interest rate on borrowing held steady at 3.31% despite substantial new PWLB borrowing at 4.57%-4.86%, indicating high refinancing costs ahead
findings.detail: New PWLB borrowing in 2025/26 was raised at 4.57%-4.86%, but the overall average rate on £481.210m borrowing remained 3.31%, matching the prior year. This stability masks the cost of new borrowing: the council took £60m at rates 126-155 basis points above the portfolio average, indicating market conditions remain expensive for new authority borrowing.
findings.matters: The high cost of new PWLB borrowing (4.57%-4.86%) reflects persistent elevated gilt yields and constrains the council's ability to finance capital programmes affordably. Future capital financing will be at similarly high rates unless the yield curve improves materially.
findings.figures: Average rate all loans 3.31%; new PWLB April 2025 4.71% (10.5 years); new PWLB Oct 2025 4.86% (13 years) and 4.57% (4 years maturity)
findings.quote: New loans totalling £60 million were taken out in 2025/26 from the Public Works Loans Board (PWLB), £30 million in April 2025 and a further £30 million in October 2025. The combined average rate of interest on existing loans and new borrowing in 2025/26 as at 31 March 2026 was unchanged at 3.31%.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Treasury Management Final Outturn
findings.headline: Council refinanced £55m of Phoenix Life loans at 0.50% saving and reduced term by 10 years, generating £7m lifetime benefit
findings.detail: In 2025/26, the council completed a second refinancing of market loans held with Phoenix Life, securing an interest rate saving of 0.50 percentage points with no premium refinancing cost. The restructured loans now have three years of interest-only payments followed by equal instalment principal repayment, rather than equal instalments throughout. The council recognized an IFRS9 accounting gain of £1.926m but reserved it as Voluntary Revenue Provision to offset future balance sheet adjustments.
findings.matters: Successful active management of existing debt indicates financial discipline and reduces long-term cost burden. The refinancing demonstrates the council's ability to access the market and renegotiate terms, a positive indicator for creditworthiness.
findings.figures: £55m refinanced at 0.50pp saving; £7m lifetime saving; loan term reduced from 29 years to 20 years (10-year reduction)
findings.quote: During 2025/26, working closely with the council's external Treasury Management advisers, the council completed a second refinancing of the £55 million of loans held with Phoenix Life. This secured an interest rate saving of 0.50 percentage points on the loans held, at no premium refinancing cost and reduced the term of the loan from twenty-nine years to twenty.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Treasury Management Final Outturn
findings.headline: Total liabilities including PFI and leases increased to £579m, up £48.5m year-on-year
findings.detail: External borrowing of £481.210m is now supplemented by £97.849m in PFI (£33.985m) and lease obligations (£63.864m under IFRS16). Total debt increased from £530.590m to £579.059m. The paper notes new vehicle and equipment leases of £10.397m and property leases of £4.379m were added in year.
findings.matters: Lease liabilities under IFRS16 are real obligations requiring revenue budget provision. The growth in recognized liabilities—particularly leases—represents commitments that constrain future budget flexibility and must be serviced before discretionary spending.
findings.figures: Total debt 31/03/2025: £530.590m; 31/03/2026: £579.059m. In-year movement: +£48.469m. Leases (vehicles/plant/property): £63.864m
findings.quote: The total debt held at 31 March 2026, including external loans, PFI and lease arrangements was £579.059 million, compared to £530.590 million on 31 March 2025.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Treasury Management Final Outturn
findings.headline: Net debt increased £38m despite capital spending being half of plan
findings.detail: The council increased net debt from £360.626m to £398.223m (up £37.597m or 10.4%) while capital expenditure fell to 48% of budget. This was driven by taking £60m in new PWLB borrowing in two tranches (April and October 2025) while capital spending remained constrained.
findings.matters: Increasing debt for capital programmes that are not being executed suggests either optimistic forecasting or a strategy of pre-positioning borrowing for future years. This raises questions about whether the council can service debt taken for capital that is deferred.
findings.figures: Net debt 31/03/2025: £360.626m; 31/03/2026: £398.223m. New PWLB borrowing £60m; debt repayments £13.560m
findings.quote: Net Debt was therefore £398.223 million, which is £38 million higher than the position at 31 March 2025, when Net Debt was £360.626 million.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Treasury Management Final Outturn
findings.headline: Capital programme significantly underspent at 48% of budget, with projects deferred to future years
findings.detail: The council budgeted £364.138m for capital expenditure but actual spend was £175.402m, a variance of -£188.736m. The report attributes this to 'reprofiling of capital expenditure, to be financed through borrowing, into future years', but does not explain why projects are being deferred or when they will proceed.
findings.matters: Large capital programme underperformance raises questions about delivery capability and project governance. For a lender, inability to execute published capital plans signals execution risk and potential service provision delays.
findings.figures: Budget £364.138m, outturn £175.402m, variance -£188.736m (52% underspend)
findings.quote: The variance between the estimated and actual outturn position largely reflects the reprofiling of capital expenditure, to be financed through borrowing, into future years.

findings.paper_title: Mainstream Budget Plans and Licensed Deficits 2026-27
findings.headline: Systemic pressure on schools from falling pupil rolls and cost inflation is driving reserve depletion: schools budgeted to use £4.047m of accumulated reserves in 2026/27
findings.detail: Maintained schools held £29.476m in reserves at 31 March 2026, but budget plans for 2026/27 anticipate using £4.047m to balance budgets (reducing reserves to £25.429m by March 2027). The broader context is that 42 of 123 schools (34%) are using reserves to balance budgets, driven by falling pupil numbers (particularly in primary) and pay costs exceeding funding increases.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion at this rate is unsustainable. Once schools exhaust reserves, they have no buffer for future pressures and will either need additional council funding or face deficit conversion to academies, amplifying the council's contingent liability.
findings.figures: £29.476m reserves at 31 March 2026; £4.047m budgeted use in 2026/27; 42 schools using reserves; 81 schools contributing to reserves
findings.quote: The budget plans agreed by schools for the 2026/27 financial year anticipate an in-year use of £4.047 million of retained balances, which would reduce retained balances to £25.429 million at 31 March 2027.

findings.paper_title: Mainstream Budget Plans and Licensed Deficits 2026-27
findings.headline: Council faces contingent liability: any school deficit remains with the council if the school converts to a sponsored academy
findings.detail: The council's legal obligations mean that when a maintained school with a deficit converts to sponsored academy status, the deficit must be written off from the council's general funds—the academy does not absorb it. The council holds a £1.795m Schools Reserve to manage this risk, but this could prove insufficient if multiple schools fail.
findings.matters: This creates an unbudgeted liability on the council's balance sheet. If Benfieldside Primary or other struggling schools fail Ofsted and require sponsorship, the council must meet the cost from general funds, directly impacting its financial position.
findings.figures: Five schools with cumulative deficits of £0.296m at 31 March 2026; Schools Reserve of £1.795m held to cover conversion deficits
findings.quote: Schools have delegated budgets, but if a school closes or converts as a sponsored academy then any deficit balance remains with the council, which must meet the cost of writing-off the deficit from its general funds.

findings.paper_title: Mainstream Budget Plans and Licensed Deficits 2026-27
findings.headline: Benfieldside Primary approved for licensed deficit due to structural decline in pupil numbers, with forecast deficits growing to £707,068 by March 2029
findings.detail: The school lost 17 pupils between 2025/26 and 2026/27 and was already in deficit (£83,187) at 31 March 2026. The approved licensed deficit for 2026/27 is £240,562, forecast to deteriorate to £450,562 by March 2028 and £707,068 by March 2029. The school has agreed to work with the authority to find a solution, but the trajectory is clearly unsustainable without intervention.
findings.matters: If this school fails an Ofsted inspection (expected for financially unsustainable schools), it must convert to a sponsored academy, at which point any deficit balance becomes a cost the council must write off from general funds—an unbudgeted liability.
findings.figures: 17 pupils lost between 2025-26 and 2026-27; deficit of £83,187 at 31 March 2026; forecast deficits of £240,562 (2027), £450,562 (2028), and £707,068 (2029)
findings.quote: The school has faced a significant reduction in pupil numbers in recent years, including a reduction of 17 pupils between 2025/26 and 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Financial Outturn report
findings.headline: Long-term borrowing costs now stand at 6%+, exceeding the council's budget assumptions of 5-5.5%
findings.detail: The council's treasury assumptions for new borrowing costs are 5-5.5%, but actual long-term borrowing costs are currently standing 'at above 6%'. This means future capital financing costs will exceed budgeted assumptions as the council moves into a position where it needs to borrow more (it has historically under-borrowed and used cash balances).
findings.matters: Rising interest rates create a forward-looking pressure on the council's budget, particularly as it depletes cash balances. This will increase the cost of the planned capital programme.
findings.figures: Long-term borrowing costs 6%+; council assumptions 5-5.5%; total debt at 31 Mar 2026 £481.210m; interest payable budget £48.021m (with £3.989m underspend in year)
findings.quote: Long term borrowing costs are currently standing at above over 6%, which exceeds the Council's assumptions on interest rates on new borrowing of between 5% and 5.5%.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Financial Outturn report
findings.headline: Capital programme slipped by £52.4m (23% of revised budget), creating reprofiling and delivery risk
findings.detail: The 2025-26 capital outturn was £175.402m against a revised budget of £227.838m, an underspend of £52.436m (23%). This represents significant slippage across multiple service areas, requiring reprofiling into future years. While underspending can reflect prudent management, the scale suggests delivery risk on capital schemes.
findings.matters: Large capital programme slippage (23%) indicates delivery challenges and creates forecasting uncertainty for future years. It may reflect scheme complexity, planning delays, or contractor issues.
findings.figures: 2025-26 capital expenditure £175.402m vs. revised budget £227.838m; underspend £52.436m (23%); total MTFP(15) capital programme £593.367m
findings.quote: The year end capital outturn for 2025/26 shows that capital expenditure totalling £175.402 million was incurred in year, £52.436 million lower than the revised capital budget reported to cabinet in March 2026. The net £52.436 million in-year underspend represents c.23% of the revised budget approved by Cabinet in March 2026.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Financial Outturn report
findings.headline: Savings delivery achieved 99.6% but some unachieved historic savings remain and are causing in-year pressures
findings.detail: The council delivered £17.961m of £18.036m (99.6%) of 2025-26 savings targets. However, the report notes there are 'unachieved savings along with previous years' MTFP savings that have not yet been fully delivered (and no alternative permanent mitigation undertaken) which are causing in year budget pressures. Action is required to be taken by the relevant services to find alternative savings options.'
findings.matters: Historic unachieved savings creating ongoing pressures suggests the council faces execution risk on its medium-term savings plans. The need to find alternative savings suggests planned reductions may not be achievable.
findings.figures: £18.036m 2025-26 savings target; £17.961m delivered (99.6%); unachieved savings causing budget pressures but figures not itemized
findings.quote: In total, £17.961 (99.6%) of the £18.036 million savings factored into the 2025/26 budget, had been delivered by 31 March 2026. The report details the unachieved savings along with previous years' MTFP savings that have not yet been fully delivered (and no alternative permanent mitigation undertaken) which are causing in year budget pressures. Action is required to be taken by the relevant services to find alternative savings options.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Financial Outturn report
findings.headline: General Fund Reserve is at the bottom of the policy range (5.89% vs. 5-7.5% policy) after £11m transfer to cover DSG liabilities
findings.detail: The closing General Fund Reserve is £39.688m, which is 5.89% of the 2026-27 net budget requirement. While this meets the minimum 5% policy threshold, it is only just within the council's stated policy range of 5-7.5%, and the position was only achieved after transferring £11m to create a new High Needs reserve. The council notes the closing reserve was £5.681m lower than forecast at quarter three.
findings.matters: A General Fund Reserve at the minimum policy threshold leaves limited headroom for unexpected pressures, particularly given the emerging CLA, highways, and school pressures identified in this report.
findings.figures: Closing General Fund Reserve £39.688m (5.89% of budget); policy range 5-7.5%; £11m transferred to High Needs reserve; £5.681m lower than Q3 forecast
findings.quote: The closing position for the General Reserve is £5.681 million lower than the position forecast at the end of quarter three, largely because of the creation of the new High Needs Stability Grant (unfunded) Reserve. The Reserves Policy specifies that General Reserves should be between 5% and 7.5% of the Council's Net Revenue Budget Requirement.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Financial Outturn report
findings.headline: Five schools ended the year in deficit; one school (Benfieldside Primary) required a licensed deficit budget with no clear path to recovery
findings.detail: Five maintained schools ended 2025-26 in deficit. Four have set budgets for 2026-27 that are forecast to return to surplus, but Benfieldside Primary 'are unable to do this and have required a licensed deficit budget to be agreed to allow them the time bring their budget back into balance over a longer period.' This suggests ongoing school sector viability issues.
findings.matters: Licensed deficits represent council underwriting of school deficits. Multiple schools requiring deficit budgets indicates structural funding or efficiency issues in the schools sector.
findings.figures: 5 schools in deficit at year-end; 1 school (Benfieldside Primary) with licensed deficit requiring multi-year recovery plan
findings.quote: Five schools ended the year in an overall deficit position. Four of these schools have set a budget in 2026/27 which will result in the school ending the 2026/27 financial year in a surplus position, whilst one school (Benfieldside Primary) are unable to do this and have required a licensed deficit budget to be agreed to allow them the time bring their budget back into balance over a longer period.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Financial Outturn report
findings.headline: Cashflowing the High Needs deficit cost the council £1.7m in lost investment income during 2025-26
findings.detail: Because the High Needs DSG deficit sits outside usable reserves as a technical negative reserve (due to Secretary of State override), the council must cashflow the cumulative deficit from its general cash balances. This foregone interest income of c. £1.7m in 2025-26 'impacts directly on the Council's General Fund and the Council Taxpayers of County Durham' and will recur as the deficit grows.
findings.matters: This is a hidden financial cost of the DSG structure that reduces the council's financial resources each year and will continue to do so. It represents deteriorating financial efficiency.
findings.figures: £1.7m loss of interest income in 2025-26; cumulative deficit requiring cashflow now £39.723m
findings.quote: In 2025/26 the Council has once again needed to cashflow this cumulative High Needs deficit, which has further reduced the council's cash balances. The loss of interest that would otherwise have been earned in 2025/26 is circa £1.700 million – impacting directly on the Council's General Fund and the Council Taxpayers of County Durham

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Financial Outturn report
findings.headline: Highways maintenance has a recurring structural overspend of £3.3m on defect repairs described as 'a recurring issue for several years'
findings.detail: Highways overspent by £1.192m in 2025-26, primarily due to £3.334m overspend on defect repairs. While £1.8m was capitalized, leaving a £1.534m net revenue overspend, the council acknowledges this is 'a recurring issue for several years'. The council is hoping the proposed Land Rental Scheme from 2026-27 will provide additional income to 'rebase the highways maintenance budget and address the structural issues within this budget area.'
findings.matters: A recurring, multi-year overspend on essential infrastructure maintenance suggests underlying underfunding or inefficiency. Reliance on a future income scheme (Land Rental) to fix the issue creates timing and realization risk.
findings.figures: £3.334m overspend on defect repairs; £1.8m capitalized; £1.534m net revenue overspend remaining
findings.quote: Highways overspent by £1.192 million to year-end. This is mainly due to overspends on highways maintenance work of £3.334 million, relating to defect repairs, which has been a recurring issue for several years. £1.8 million of this overspend has however been mitigated by capitalising some Highway Maintenance costs where suitable opportunities arise, leaving an overspend on revenue maintenance of £1.534 million.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Financial Outturn report
findings.headline: Aycliffe Secure Centre received Ofsted 'Inadequate' rating and is forecast to exceed its remaining £0.186m reserve in 2026-27
findings.detail: The Aycliffe Secure Centre received an Inadequate Ofsted inspection rating in December 2025, reducing occupancy and income. It used £0.710m of reserves in 2025-26 to balance the position and has only £0.186m in reserves remaining. The council states "it is likely the in-year deficit will exceed this level, resulting in a financial pressure for the wider CYPS budget next year, which may require corporate support through the General Fund Reserve." An Ofsted re-assessment in March 2026 improved the rating to 'Requires Improvement', allowing occupancy increases ahead.
findings.matters: An Ofsted-driven reduction in income from a secure services facility creates both immediate and ongoing financial risk. Reliance on General Fund reserves to cover deficits indicates this service is currently unviable at break-even.
findings.figures: £0.710m reserve used in 2025-26; £0.186m reserves remaining; Ofsted rating: Inadequate (December 2025), then Requires Improvement (March 2026)
findings.quote: The Aycliffe Secure Centre (ASC) used £0.710 million of its earmarked reserves to balance the in-year financial position. Income levels were significantly lower than budget, as the number of beds occupied during the final quarter of the year was relatively low, following the "Inadequate" Ofsted judgement from the inspection in December 2025... ASC has reserves of £0.186 million to carry forward to support the financial position in 2026/27, however it is likely the in-year deficit will exceed this level, resulting in a financial pressure for the wider CYPS budget next year, which may require corporate support through the General Fund Reserve.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Financial Outturn report
findings.headline: Children Looked After placements overspent by £5.6m with a 12% increase in numbers and £31m cost pressures forecast across the medium term
findings.detail: The Children Looked After budget overspent by £5.588m in 2025-26. The number of placements increased by 147 children (12%) during the year, from 1,182 to 1,329. External residential placements (the most expensive type) were £2.621m over budget despite lower-than-forecast in-house availability. The council has identified £31m of cost pressures it is attempting to mitigate through the Durham Cares Sufficiency Programme Board.
findings.matters: Sustained demand growth (12% year-on-year) in a high-cost service with significant projected medium-term pressures suggests this will remain a structural budget issue. Delays to mitigation measures create continued overspend risk.
findings.figures: £5.588m overspend in year; 147 additional placements (12% increase); external residential placements £2.621m over budget; £31m total cost pressures forecast across MTFP; average cost £0.379m per external residential placement
findings.quote: The largest area of spending within CYPS relates to Children Looked After (CLA) placements costs, where the net budget for 2025/26 was £97.346 million, £20.295 million higher than in 2024/25. At year end there was an of overspend of £5.588 million against this budget. Over the year, the number of CLA placements has increased by 147 (12%), from 1,182 at the start of the year to 1,329 at the end.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Financial Outturn report
findings.headline: Special Educational Needs DSG deficit has grown to £39.7m with the council still facing a £4m unfunded liability after government support
findings.detail: The High Needs Block cumulative deficit increased by £16.742m in year to £39.723m. While the government announced it would fund 90% through a new High Needs Stability Grant (subject to approval of a SEND Reform Plan), the council must fund the remaining 10% (c. £3.972m of existing deficit, plus £7m more forecast in 2026-27 and 2027-28). The council has created an £11m reserve to cover this shortfall.
findings.matters: A £40m+ DSG deficit represents a structural funding gap that will require ongoing council reserves, and the government funding is conditional on approval of a reform plan. This is a medium-term liability affecting financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Cumulative deficit £39.723m (increased from £22.981m); government funding up to £35.751m (90%); council minimum unfunded liability c. £4m current + £7m future; £11m reserve created
findings.quote: Should the Government ultimately fund the writing-off of 90% of this accumulated deficit (c.£35.751 million) then the Council will need to meet (as a minimum) c. £3.972 million of this. Significant in-year deficits are forecast to be accrued in 2026/27 (c. £30 million) and 2027/28 (c. £40 million), meaning that a further (minimum) £7 million will need to be met by the Council, which is why the £11 million High Needs Stability Grant (unfunded) Reserve has been created.

findings.paper_title: 09 Annual Internal Audit Opinion and Internal Audit Report 2526
findings.headline: Internal Audit capacity compromised: only 81% of planned work delivered
findings.detail: Internal Audit delivered only 81% of planned productive days (2,942 of 3,629 planned) against a 90% target. The service operated with two long-term unplanned staff absences and a vacant Audit Assistant post throughout 2025/26, directly impacting service capacity and ability to deliver planned coverage.
findings.matters: An understaffed internal audit function means fewer control weaknesses are being detected. Understaffing also signals broader resource pressures affecting the council's operations.
findings.figures: 2,942 productive days delivered of 3,629 planned (81%); approximately 85% of audit plan delivered
findings.quote: Throughout the year, the service continued to operate with two long term unplanned staff absences as well as a vacant Audit Assistant post, which have directly impacted on service capacity and the ability to deliver all of the planned work in the 2025/26 Audit Plan.

findings.paper_title: 09 Annual Internal Audit Opinion and Internal Audit Report 2526
findings.headline: Weak contract management across the council creating financial and operational risk
findings.detail: Internal Audit identified weak contract management including poorly embedded practices, weak performance monitoring and oversight, and inaccurate contract registers. Testing found significant inconsistencies in how contract management controls were applied. This spans transport, property, and procurement areas.
findings.matters: Weak contract management directly enables fraud, overpayment, and loss of value for money. It also indicates a broader control culture failure across the organisation.
findings.figures: Eight audits identified contract management weaknesses; Limited Assurance opinions for transport contracts, corporate property, and contract register
findings.quote: The organisation has a broadly sound control framework, but key risks arise from inconsistent application, weak contract management, and compliance failures.

findings.paper_title: 09 Annual Internal Audit Opinion and Internal Audit Report 2526
findings.headline: Transport contractors overpaid £20,489: £13,577 for journeys not undertaken, £6,912 from calculation errors
findings.detail: The council overpaid transport contractors £13,577 for journeys not undertaken and £6,912 from calculation errors in uplift payments. Key school attendance verification controls were removed post-Covid. The council relied on unverified contractor invoices. As of the audit date, £923k in invoices remained on hold and disputes aged over 12 months.
findings.matters: Control breakdowns enabled direct financial losses. Removal of key controls and reliance on unverified invoices represents deteriorated risk management in major operational spending.
findings.figures: £13,577 overpayment for journeys not undertaken; £6,912 from calculation errors; £923k invoices on hold

findings.paper_title: 01. MTFP(16) County Council 18.02.2026
findings.headline: General Reserve at minimum threshold of 5.3% (£35.914 million) and earmarked reserves down 20.91% over three years, limiting financial resilience
findings.detail: The council's General Reserve is forecast at £35.914 million on 31 March 2026, representing 5.3% of the Net Revenue Budget Requirement. This is at the bottom of the council's own policy range of 5%-7.5% and above the minimum threshold, but it leaves little buffer for unforeseen events. More concerning, earmarked reserves have declined by 20.91% over the three years to March 2025 (though the document notes the council's position remains relatively strong compared to other unitary authorities). The combination of minimal general reserves, declining earmarked reserves, and a £44.745 million structural deficit over 2027-30 leaves the council vulnerable to any adverse financial event.
findings.matters: Reserves are a critical measure of financial resilience. A council at the minimum threshold of its own reserves policy has limited room to absorb shocks, unexpected cost pressures, or grant reductions. Given the structural deficit ahead and High Needs deficits still being cash-flowed, reserve headroom is constrained.
findings.figures: General Reserve forecast: £35.914 million (31 March 2026); percentage of budget: 5.3%; policy range: 5%-7.5%; cash range for 2026/27: £33.703m-£50.555m; earmarked reserves: £155.3 million; decline in reserves over 3 years to March 2025: 20.91%
findings.quote: Current forecasts indicate that the General Reserve will be £35.914 million on 31 March 2026, above the minimum threshold set out in the Reserves Policy agreed by Council and representing 5.3% of next year's Net Revenue Budget Requirement

findings.paper_title: 01. MTFP(16) County Council 18.02.2026
findings.headline: Pupil numbers declining 1.8% year-on-year with schools funding following pupils, creating structural revenue reduction
findings.detail: Pupil numbers in County Durham have fallen by 1,152 pupils (1.8%) between the October 2024 and October 2025 censuses, with particularly sharp declines in primary schools. Because school funding formulas allocate at least 80% of funding by pupil numbers, this decline directly reduces the Schools Block allocation year-on-year. Growth funding (additional allocation for rapidly expanding schools) will not be applied in 2026/27, further tightening school budgets. Declining pupil numbers are a structural, demographic headwind that will persist across multiple years.
findings.matters: Unlike demand-driven pressures (social care, SEND) that can be offset by investment, demographic decline in pupil numbers is a revenue reduction the council must absorb through service cuts or efficiency gains. This is a headwind running counter to inflation and pay award growth, making it harder to balance overall budgets.
findings.figures: Pupil number decline: 1,152 pupils (1.8%) between Oct 2024 and Oct 2025 censuses; sharpest declines in primary sector; growth funding not applied in 2026/27; at least 80% of school funding allocation is pupil-led
findings.quote: In County Durham, pupil numbers have fallen by 1,152 (1.8%) between the October 2024 and October 2025 censuses, with the sharpest declines in the primary sector. As pupil-led factors form most of the school funding allocations, this reduction has materially diminished Schools Block allocations year-on-year

findings.paper_title: 01. MTFP(16) County Council 18.02.2026
findings.headline: Council withdrawn £0.250 million saving from Household Waste Recycling Centres rationalisation following consultation feedback
findings.detail: Cabinet have withdrawn a proposed saving of £0.250 million (£0.125 million in 2027/28 and £0.125 million in 2028/29) linked to a review and rationalisation of Household Waste Recycling Centres following consideration of consultation responses. The withdrawal suggests consultation pushback on service reductions and indicates the council was unable or unwilling to proceed with the proposal. This is a relatively small amount but signals potential difficulty in delivering wider savings plans.
findings.matters: A council that withdraws savings proposals after consultation demonstrates responsiveness to public concern but also reveals limits on further savings from this area. If other savings proposals face similar resistance, the council's ability to deliver its full £15.469 million savings programme (which is already heavily front-loaded to 2026/27) becomes a delivery risk.

findings.quote: Cabinet have withdrawn the saving linked to a review and rationalisation of Household Waste Recycling Facilities (with these proposals originally assuming £0.125 million would be saved in 2027/28 and £0.125 million in 2028/29)

findings.paper_title: 01. MTFP(16) County Council 18.02.2026
findings.headline: Large capital programme of £263.666 million over 4 years creates pre-commitment of £3.6 million annual capital financing costs extending to 2031/32
findings.detail: The council is approving £263.666 million of new capital investments over 2026/27-2029/30: £147.766 million funded by corporate borrowing, £2.600 million by self-financing borrowing, and £113.300 million by grants. Major schemes include £26 million for Villa Real special school, £33.5 million for special educational provision, £47 million for highways maintenance. These borrowings create a pre-commitment of approximately £3.6 million of annual revenue capital financing costs that extend into 2031/32 (outside the current MTFP period). This locks in borrowing costs during a period when the council already faces a £44.745 million structural deficit.
findings.matters: Heavy capital borrowing (£150.366 million over 4 years) increases the council's debt service burden precisely when revenue budgets are under severe pressure. The extension of costs to 2031/32 means future administrations will inherit these commitments. A lender needs to assess whether the council's debt sustainability is manageable given the concurrent structural revenue deficit.

findings.paper_title: 01. MTFP(16) County Council 18.02.2026
findings.headline: Social care precept covers only 20.6% of unavoidable Adult and Children's social care budget growth of £29.749 million
findings.detail: The council faces £29.749 million in unavoidable social care budget growth: £10.005 million in Adult Social Care and £19.744 million in Children's Social Care placement pressures. A 1.99% council tax increase (entirely Social Care Precept) generates only £6.129 million, covering just 20.6% of these pressures. The council is therefore absorbing £23.6 million of social care cost growth through redirected funding, service reductions, or use of reserves. Children's placement costs (£19.744 million) are a particular pressure point.
findings.matters: Placement cost pressures in children's social care suggest increasing caseload complexity, higher external provider costs, or both. This is a demand-driven cost that the council cannot control and suggests underlying service pressures will persist. The gap between cost growth and council tax funding creates an ongoing structural mismatch.

findings.paper_title: 01. MTFP(16) County Council 18.02.2026
findings.headline: Temporary government Recovery Grant Uplift cliff: £4.885 million funding withdrawn in 2028/29 after £3.745 million added in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council receives additional core funding via the Recovery Grant Uplift Grant to address years of underfunding: £3.745 million in 2026/27, increasing to £4.885 million in 2027/28, then dropping sharply to £1.370 million in 2028/29 (a loss of £3.515 million year-on-year). The council has factored this into MTFP projections but has not identified how to replace the lost funding.
findings.matters: The council is factoring temporary funding into structural spending plans. Without a permanent replacement (either from government or local revenue raising), this creates a predictable cliff that will force further savings or council tax rises in 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: 01. MTFP(16) County Council 18.02.2026
findings.headline: Structural budget deficit of £44.745 million across 2027/28-2029/30 with 47% of pressure in 2028/29 and no funding solution identified

This is being addressed in the MTFP(17) planning process.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether a council can balance its books without repeated reserve drawdowns (which are not sustainable) or unaffordable council tax rises. findings.paper_title: 01. MTFP(16) County Council 18.02.2026
findings.headline: High Needs SEND deficit cumulative reach £39.710 million by March 2026 with 10% balance (circa £4m) left unfunded after 90% government write-off

The in-year deficits are forecast to worsen to £20-£25 million in 2026/27 and 2027/28.

findings.quote: A significant and escalating financial risk to the Council's reserves position, and to that of the wider sector, relates to the High Needs Block (HNB), where in year deficits for this council are forecast to rise to £16.729 million in 2025/26, with a cumulative deficit of £39.710 million by March 2026

findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report
findings.headline: The council is committed to £405m of new borrowing through 2028/29 plus a further £150m for new capital schemes, at a time when long-term rates are around 6%.

A further £150.4m of borrowing is required for new capital spending commitments. Long-term PWLB rates remain high at around 6% for 40-year borrowing. Capital financing costs are rising as a percentage of the revenue budget, with pre-commitments of £3.6m of capital financing costs needed in 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report
findings.headline: The council must fund 10% of its accumulated High Needs Block deficit despite government write-off of 90%, with uncertainty on timing and amount of grant payments.

The receipt of grant funding is subject to agreement of a local SEND Reform Plan (details not yet published), so it is unclear whether all accumulated costs will be eligible. Interest costs on cash-flowing the deficit are £1.7m in 2025/26 and expected to reach £2.5m in 2026/27.
findings.matters: The High Needs deficit is a contingent liability that sits on the council's balance sheet. Even after the government write-off, the council faces a multi-million pound ongoing drain on resources and uncertainty about the final settlement, which could impact future financial plans.

findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report
findings.headline: Adult Social Care spending increases £10.005m in 2026/27 for 4.1% National Living Wage rise; MTFP assumes 3.7%, 2.9%, 2.7% in following years
findings.detail: The council must increase Adult Social Care spending by £10.005m in 2026/27 due to the confirmed 4.1% National Living Wage rise. The Section 151 Officer notes that each 1% of National Living Wage rise adds around £1.4m to adult social care costs. The MTFP assumes later-year wage increases of 3.7%, 2.9% and 2.7% in years 2-4, but acknowledges these may prove insufficient given national wage inflation currently running at 4.5%. The report also notes planned increases in demographic pressures subject to potential volatility.
findings.matters: Social care cost pressures are a key vulnerability for many councils. If wage inflation persists above assumptions, adult social care costs could escalate rapidly, forcing either further service cuts or additional council tax rises.
findings.figures: 2026/27 Adult Social Care increase: £10.005m; National Living Wage rise April 2026: 4.1%; cost per 1% NLW rise: £1.4m; MTFP assumptions 2027/28-2029/30: 3.7%, 2.9%, 2.7%; current national wage inflation: 4.5%

findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report
findings.headline: The council's core spending power growth depends heavily on raising council tax by the maximum permitted amount, but it is only increasing by 1.99%.
findings.detail: Government calculations assume councils will raise council tax by 5% per annum to help fund statutory social care pressures. For County Durham, 52.6% of the reported Core Spending Power increase over three years is derived from assumed maximum 5% council tax rises, while only 47.4% comes from government grant. However, the council is proposing only a 1.99% increase, well below the permitted 4.99%. This means the council is forgoing £6.1m of assumed funding in 2026/27 alone.
findings.matters: This reveals a structural mismatch between government funding assumptions and the council's ability or willingness to raise council tax. The gap must be closed through reserves or savings, both of which create financial vulnerability.
findings.figures: Government assumption: 5% council tax rise per annum; Council proposal: 1.99%; permitted maximum: 4.99%; funding gap 2026/27: £6.129m; proportion of Core Spending Power from assumed council tax rises: 52.6%
findings.quote: 52.6% of the reported increase in Core Spending Power over the next three years is derived from assumed maximum 5% per annum increases in Council Tax, which is funding raised locally, and not central government support by way of additional grant income. Therefore only 47.4% of core spending power increases across the period are assumed to be from increased grant funding.

findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report
findings.headline: Reserves have declined 30% since March 2021 and are now at the bottom of the council's target range, leaving limited financial resilience.
findings.detail: Total reserves (excluding schools) have fallen from £271.7m in March 2021 to a forecast £191.2m in March 2026, a 30% decline. General Fund reserves are forecast at £35.9m (5.76% of budget), which sits within the council's 5-7.5% target but at the lower end. Reserves as a percentage of net budget have fallen from 41.1% in March 2024 to 37.3% in March 2025. The CIPFA Financial Resilience Index notes concerning trends in reserve reduction across the wider local government sector.
findings.matters: Declining reserves are an early warning sign of financial distress. A council operating at the bottom of its reserve target range has minimal buffer for unexpected shocks, making it more vulnerable to service interruption or further deterioration.
findings.figures: Total reserves 31 March 2021: £271.682m; forecast 31 March 2026: £191.180m; decline: 30%; General Fund Reserve forecast 31 March 2026: £35.914m (5.76% of NRB); target range 2026/27: £33.703m-£50.555m
findings.quote: Since 31 March 2021, when reserves held were £271.682 million, when compared to the forecast position to 31 March 2026, the overall levels of reserves held is forecast to have declined by 30%.

findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report
findings.headline: The council faces a structural deficit of £44.7m from 2027/28 to 2029/30, requiring either major council tax rises or transformational service cuts.

The Section 151 Officer warns this will likely increase when 2027/28 forecasts are updated. Bridging this gap will require either sustained council tax increases above inflation or major service transformation.
findings.matters: This reveals a structural imbalance in the council's finances, not a one-off problem. The scale of the future deficit means the council's financial stability depends on being able to implement substantial savings or secure permission for above-inflation council tax rises, both of which carry execution and political risks.
findings.figures: MTFP(16) deficit 2027/28-2029/30: £44.745m; MTFP Support Reserve balance 31 March 2026: £34.576m; each 1% council tax increase generates: £3.079m

findings.paper_title: Section 25 Report
findings.headline: Children's looked after placements budget has grown unsustainably and is the primary driver of council financial difficulty.

The 2026/27 budget is being increased by a further £19.4m to £116.8m, representing a 382% increase over eight years. By the end of the medium-term plan, this single budget is forecast to exceed £127m.
findings.matters: Lenders assessing covenant strength need to understand that this council is facing unsustainable cost escalation in a statutory service where the council itself states the budget cannot continue on this trajectory. This is the stated primary cause of recent financial difficulties.

findings.quote: This scale of budget increase is simply unsustainable, with increases in this budget being the primary cause of the financial difficulties faced by the Council in recent years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - DCC Annual Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026-27
findings.headline: Total gross debt forecast to grow 33% to £703m by March 2027, with £405m of planned new borrowing
findings.detail: Gross debt is forecast to increase from £530.6m (March 2025) to £703.3m (March 2027). The strategy explicitly plans to draw down £405m in new PWLB loans over 2026/27 and 2028/29. findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - DCC Annual Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026-27
findings.headline: Council strategy to deplete reserves to avoid borrowing at high interest rates
findings.detail: The council is deliberately running down investment balances (reserves) to fund capital expenditure rather than borrow at current elevated rates. Investment balances are falling from £138.1m in December 2025 to an expected £41.5m by March 2026 — a reduction of £96.6m in three months. This materially weakens the council's financial cushion.
findings.matters: Reserves are essential for financial resilience and flexibility. Rapid depletion reduces the council's ability to manage cash flow volatility, fund emergencies, or absorb service cost pressures without additional borrowing. This also leaves less scope for internal borrowing in future years.
findings.figures: Total investments falling from £138.089m (31/12/2025) to £41.500m (31/03/2026 estimate); net debt position worsening from £349.945m to £436.755m

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - DCC Annual Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026-27
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing by £251m (32.6%) in one year to £1,023m
findings.detail: The CFR is projected to jump from £771.7m to £1,023m between March 2026 and March 2027. CFR represents the council's underlying borrowing need. While some growth reflects capital expenditure and IFRS 16 lease accounting treatment, this scale of one-year increase (£251m) is substantial and signals a significant shift in the council's debt profile.
findings.matters: CFR is the fundamental measure of a council's debt burden and trajectory. A 32% one-year increase raises questions about sustainability and future affordability. Lenders monitor CFR trends to assess whether debt is growing faster than the council's capacity to service it.
findings.figures: Opening CFR 2025/26 £771.725m, Closing CFR 2026/27 £1,022.969m, movement £251.244m

findings.paper_title: Appendix 12 - DCC Annual Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026-27
findings.headline: Capital expenditure planned at £337.8m for 2026/27, the largest annual spend in the forecast period
findings.detail: Capital expenditure is forecast to peak at £337.8m in 2026/27, up from £227.7m in 2025/26 and falling back to £157.3m in 2027/28. This concentrated spike in a single year suggests a major programme of asset investment or renewal. The strategy does not explain what this capital is being deployed for.
findings.matters: Large one-year capital spikes indicate major asset investment decisions and require substantial financing. A lender needs to understand the nature of these assets, their expected useful lives, and whether they generate revenue or savings to service the debt.

findings.detail: Paragraph 15 states 'If an investment is considered to be underperforming, or no longer meets the key objectives, then an exit strategy will be prepared.' This signals the council expects some properties may not deliver intended returns.
findings.matters: While exit planning is prudent, the anticipation of underperformance suggests the council may need to realise losses on some of its income-generating assets

findings.detail: The strategy notes that while local authority property investment has grown over ten years, 'more recently, there has been increased focus on these decisions and investments, where in some authorities the commercial risks take on has proved unsustainable.' The council claims it will apply a 'cautious approach' and 'robust risk assessment'.

findings.paper_title: 06 Audit Completion Report 202425 Durham County Council Pension Fund
findings.headline: Pension fund records contain unresolved discrepancies of £4.7m in investment valuations against fund managers' records.
findings.detail: Auditors identified £2.945m difference between Border to Coast Pensions Partnership's valuations of Level 3 investments and the fund's records, and £1.744m difference between CBRE's pooled property valuations and the fund's records. While assessed individually and collectively as immaterial, these unadjusted misstatements remain in the accounts and indicate ongoing reconciliation weaknesses between the fund's records and external managers.
findings.matters: Persistent discrepancies in asset valuations create a control gap; if such differences accumulate undetected, they could eventually become material and undermine the accuracy of the fund's financial position.

findings.paper_title: 06 Audit Completion Report 202425 Durham County Council Pension Fund
findings.headline: Pension fund accounting team skipped monthly reconciliations throughout 2024/25 due to staff shortages, completing them only at year-end.
findings.detail: Monthly reconciliations of contributions receivable, investment book costs, investment income, and bank reconciliations for leavers' payments were not completed in each month during 2024/25 due to staffing constraints. All reconciliations were deferred to year-end closedown. Management has since appointed new staff and describes the team as now fully resourced.
findings.matters: Extended gaps in monthly reconciliations increase the risk of undetected errors accumulating; even though this issue has been addressed through hiring, it signals prior resource constraints in a key financial control function.
findings.figures: Reconciliation delays described as due to 'staff long-term absence and staff shortages within the Pensions Accountancy team during 2024/25'; four separate monthly reconciliation processes were affected.
findings.quote: Due to a staff long-term absence and staff shortages within the Pensions Accountancy team during 2024/25, the reconciliation was rescheduled for completion at the year-end. New staff members have been appointed, and the team is now fully resourced.

findings.paper_title: 11 Strategic Risk Management Progress Report for 2025-26 - Review 2
findings.headline: Educational Psychologist vacancy rate of 37% (10.74 FTE unfilled) creating delays in statutory Education, Health and Care assessments.
findings.detail: The ability to deliver timely statutory Education, Health and Care (EHC) assessments is at risk. As of 1 August 2025, the Educational Psychologist vacancy rate stands at 37%, with 10.74 FTE posts unfilled out of 29.99 FTE establishment. This shortage is part of a wider national and regional issue, compounded by rising post-Covid demand. The service has secured £390,000 growth funding for 2025-26 to create four new posts, and is recruiting internationally (two Educational Psychologists from South Africa recruited). However, demand remains high and capacity within the permanent workforce is insufficient to meet statutory timescales.
findings.matters: Failure to meet statutory timescales for EHC assessments can trigger legal challenges and reputational damage. This is a capacity constraint that directly impacts service delivery to vulnerable children.
findings.figures: 37% vacancy rate as of 1 August 2025; 10.74 FTE unfilled out of 29.99 FTE establishment; £390,000 growth funding for 2025-26; four new posts created; two international hires from South Africa
findings.quote: As of 1 August 2025, the vacancy rate stands at 37%, with 10.74 FTE posts unfilled out of an establishment of 29.99 FTE. This shortage is part of a wider national and regional issue, compounded by rising demand for assessments post-Covid. Although temporary funding previously enabled the use of temporary agency support to clear backlogs, demand remains high and capacity within the permanent workforce is insufficient to meet statutory timescales.

findings.paper_title: 11 Strategic Risk Management Progress Report for 2025-26 - Review 2
findings.headline: Health and Social Care Reforms risk elevated to Corporate Key Risk due to ICB restructuring and government funding uncertainty.
findings.detail: CR-AHS-1 has been uprated from Major/Possible (Net Risk Score 36) to Major/Probable (Net Risk Score 48) and is now a Corporate Key Risk. The risk stems from government changes to commissioning and integration arrangements for health and social care. Ongoing restructuring has reduced local resources and shifted decision-making centrally. As of May 2025, further changes are being developed by Government. More detail is expected by Autumn 2025, but reductions in funding or commissioning capacity may impact health outcomes, joint funding arrangements (Better Care Fund, Continuing Health Care), and service integration.
findings.matters: Health and social care is a material cost area for councils and joint funding arrangements underpin adult safeguarding. Funding reductions directly impact the council's ability to commission services.
findings.figures: Uprated from Major/Possible (Net Risk Score 36) to Major/Probable (Net Risk Score 48); risk flagged at Autumn 2025 for further clarity on ICB and funding changes
findings.quote: Health and Social Care Reforms is elevated due to the restructuring of the Integrated Care Board (ICB), from Major/Possible with a (Net Risk Score of 36) to Major/Probable and a (Net Risk Score of 48). Ongoing restructuring has reduced local resources and shifted decision-making centrally. As of May 2025, further changes are being developed by Government, with local ICB leaders working to realign structures and budgets. More detail is expected by Autumn 2025, but reductions in funding or commissioning capacity may impact health outcomes, joint funding arrangements (e.g. Better Care Fund, Continuing Health Care), and service integration.

findings.paper_title: 11 Strategic Risk Management Progress Report for 2025-26 - Review 2
findings.headline: £45.8 million funding gap over 2025/26-2028/29, expanding to £71 million if Council Tax is frozen from 2026/27.
findings.detail: The council forecasts a funding gap of £45.848 million across 2025/26 to 2028/29, driven by sustained demand and inflationary pressures in children's and adult social care, school transport, capital financing, and national living wage costs. This gap assumes annual Council Tax increases of 2.99%. If Council Tax is not increased from 2026/27 onwards, the gap potentially expands to £71 million. The council is developing savings proposals of £18.036 million in 2025/26 and £23.404 million across the MTFP period.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility of the council's ability to balance budgets without excessive reserve drawdown. The funding gap depends on Fair Funding Review 2.0 outcomes (uncertain) and Council Tax policy decisions outside the council's direct control.
findings.figures: £45.848 million funding gap 2025/26-2028/29; £71 million if Council Tax frozen; £18.036 million savings 2025/26; £23.404 million savings across four-year MTFP; assumes 2.99% annual Council Tax increase
findings.quote: A funding gap of £45.848 million is forecast across the period 2025/26 to 2028/29, driven by sustained demand and inflationary pressures in areas such as children's and adult social care, school transport, capital financing, and national living wage costs... any decision not to increase Council Tax from 2026/27 onwards will widen the gap further, potentially requiring £71 million in savings over the four-year period if Council Tax remains frozen.

findings.paper_title: 11 Strategic Risk Management Progress Report for 2025-26 - Review 2
findings.headline: HNB SEND cumulative deficit forecast to reach £85 million by end 2027/28, with statutory accounting override expiring 31 March 2028.
findings.detail: Increasing demand for special educational needs services, driven by earlier diagnosis and wider eligibility following 2014 SEND reforms, is outpacing the High Needs Block budget. The cumulative deficit is forecast at £85 million by 2027/28. The council's Statement of Going Concern explicitly identifies this as 'a serious and continuing concern.' The statutory accounting override that currently allows councils to exclude HNB deficits from general revenue position expires 31 March 2028. Without government funding, removal will place substantial pressure on reserves and could force Section 114 notices.
findings.matters: This is an explicit going concern risk. The end of the accounting override in 2028 means the deficit hits the general revenue account unless government provides funding, forcing reserve drawdown or a budget crisis.
findings.figures: £85 million cumulative deficit by end 2027/28; £2 million cost reduction target by 2026/27; £1 billion national uplift to High Needs Block confirmed; Phase 1 of Sustainability Programme delivered
findings.quote: The cumulative deficit is forecast to reach £85 million by the end of 2027/28, with significant implications for the Council's Medium Term Financial Plan (MTFP) and overall financial resilience. This aligns with the Council's Statement of Going Concern, which identifies the HNB/SEND deficit as a serious and continuing concern.

findings.paper_title: 05 Audit Completion Report 202425 Durham County Council
findings.headline: A known 2021/22 valuation error affecting five land assets remains uncorrected in the balance sheet
findings.detail: Five land assets were incorrectly valued using actual area instead of modern equivalent asset area in calculations. This error was identified in 2021/22, carried forward as unadjusted through 2023/24, and has not been corrected in 2024/25 because none of these five assets were selected for revaluation in the current year's rolling programme.
findings.matters: The failure to remediate a known error across three consecutive years indicates weak processes for tracking audit findings and ensuring their resolution, suggesting deficiencies in the council's financial governance.
findings.figures: £1.015m unadjusted in 2024/25
findings.quote: Our review confirmed that none of the five assets noted above have been reviewed during 2024/25 and therefore the issue remains in relation to these.

findings.paper_title: 05 Audit Completion Report 202425 Durham County Council
findings.headline: Property valuation control deficiency identified in the prior year has not been resolved
findings.detail: The auditors note: 'In the prior year we identified weaknesses in terms of overall responsibility and control over the valuation process.' Despite the council implementing quality assurance checks, the 2024/25 testing found these checks remain insufficient to catch errors in the external valuer's work. This affects land and buildings valued at £988.9m and surplus assets of £46.2m, the council's largest asset classes.
findings.matters: A recurring control deficiency over the council's largest asset holdings signals weak oversight of financial reporting in a material area, raising questions about the reliability of reported asset values and the council's overall control environment.
findings.figures: £988.9m land and buildings; £46.2m surplus assets
findings.quote: Although the Council has implemented a number of quality assurance checks, the findings from our testing did not indicate that checks had been sufficient to pick up the errors made by the external valuer. As in the previous year, we consider that checks should have been carried out when the initial valuations were received from the external valuer.

findings.paper_title: 05 Audit Completion Report 202425 Durham County Council
findings.headline: £8.9m of unadjusted property valuation errors remain in the 2024/25 financial statements
findings.detail: The auditors identified and reported two populations of uncorrected valuation errors: £2.592m in depreciated replacement cost (DRC) valued assets that are overstated, and £4.520m in existing use value (EUV) assets that are understated. Additionally, a £1.015m error carried forward from 2021/22 remains unadjusted. Management has assessed these as not material individually or in aggregate and chosen not to correct them.

news_drafts.headline: Durham highways overspent by £1.192m in 2025/26, driven by £3.334m on road defect repairs
news_drafts.lead:
Durham County Council's highways service overspent its day-to-day budget by £1.192m in 2025/26, according to a report to the Environment and Sustainable Communities Overview and Scrutiny Committee, which met on 2 October. Day-to-day spending (revenue spending) covers staff, services and contracts, as opposed to spending on things that last.

The report says the overspend was mainly due to £3.334m spent over budget on highways maintenance, specifically repairing defects in the road network. It describes this as "a recurring issue for several years". Where the work qualified, the council paid for £1.8m of the repairs as capital spending, which is money spent on things that last, such as roads. That left £1.534m of the defect repair overspend falling on the day-to-day budget.

For the structural gap in the highways budget, the council plans a new Land Rental Scheme, which the report says will start in 2026/27.

news_drafts.headline: County Durham Council assessed as a "going concern" on 31 July, with no significant risks identified
news_drafts.lead:
County Durham Council's Corporate Director of Resources concluded on 31 July 2026 that the council can be treated as a "going concern", meaning an organisation expected to keep operating, which is the basis on which its formal annual accounts (the statement of accounts) are prepared. The assessment found the council has "a history of stable finance and ready access to financial resources in the future".

It also found no significant financial, operating or other risks that would jeopardise the council's continuing operation, and that the accounts could be prepared on that basis. The papers record the conclusion only. They put no figures on it.

The assessment is set out in the annual report of the council's Audit Committee, covering September 2025 to August 2026, which was before the committee at its meeting on 30 September 2026.

news_drafts.headline: County Durham's schools high needs overspend was £16.7m in 2025-26 against £14.25m budgeted
news_drafts.lead:
County Durham's spending on support for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) overspent by £16.742m in 2025-26, the Children and Young People's Overview and Scrutiny Committee was told on 25 September. The council had budgeted for a deficit of £14.250m on the high needs part of the dedicated schools grant (the government money that funds schools, with high needs covering children with SEND). The outturn, the actual figures once the year had ended, was £2.492m worse. The overall schools-funding deficit stood at £36.080m at the year end, up from £20.229m.

The papers attribute part of the overspend to alternative provision, which exceeded budget by £1.754m, and to post-16 independent and non-maintained special schools, which overspent by £0.830m because demand was higher than anticipated. For 2026-27, the council set the high needs budget with a deficit of £30.278m. The first-quarter forecast is £31.105m, or £0.827m higher, because of more special school places and higher costs for pupils with complex needs. On that forecast the cumulative deficit reaches £67.185m by 31 March 2027.

The council submitted its Local SEND Reform Plan to the Department for Education in June 2026. Once the plan is assessed and approved, funding of up to 90% of the £36.080m deficit, or £32.472m, would be paid to the council, leaving about £3.6m. The statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps such deficits off the main balance sheet, expires on 31 March 2028, when the paper says central government assumes responsibility for SEND funding.
